page.title: Content Marketing Operations Services Explained
page.description: What content marketing operations services cover, from workflow design and tool selection to publishing cadence and performance reporting.
page.h1: What is included in content marketing operations services?
page.definition: Content marketing operations services are the systems, workflows and governance that move content from brief to publish and measure its impact. They cover intake, production, review, approval, publishing and reporting across owned channels.
page.quick_answer: Start by mapping your current intake-to-publish flow, then assign one owner to each of the seven stages so nothing stalls in review.

sections.h2: Which stages make up a content operations workflow?

blocks.p: Seven stages, each with one owner and one output, keep work moving from idea to insight: intake, brief, production, review, approval, publishing, reporting.

ol: Intake captures requests and assigns priority
Brief defines audience, angle, format and deadline
Production creates draft assets and copy
Review gathers structured feedback from stakeholders
Approval locks the final version with a named sign-off
Publishing pushes to CMS, email, social and syndication
Reporting ties performance back to the brief goals

sections.h2: What tools do teams use to run content operations?

blocks.p: Teams typically combine a work management tool, a brief repository, a publishing platform and an analytics layer.

sections.h2: How long does a typical content cycle take?

blocks.p: A realistic cycle for a long-form article is five to ten working days from approved brief to publish, with most time spent in review and approval.

ul: Brief to first draft: two to four days
Review rounds: two to five days depending on stakeholder count
Approval and CMS entry: one day
First performance read: 48 hours after publish

blocks.p: Clear ownership, SLAs for each stage and a single source of truth for the calendar stop work from piling up in review.

ul: One named owner per stage with authority to move work forward
Maximum two review rounds before escalation
Shared editorial calendar visible to all contributors
Monthly retrospective on cycle time and revision count
Capacity plan that matches publishing cadence to available writers

sections.h2: How do you measure content operations health?

blocks.p: Track four core metrics that reveal whether the system is delivering on time and improving over time.

ul: Cycle time from brief to publish
Capacity utilisation across writers and editors

sections.h2: When should you bring in outside help?

blocks.p: Engage a specialist when internal teams lack bandwidth to design the workflow, select tools or run the monthly operations review.

ul: Launching a new content programme with no existing process
Scaling output beyond current team capacity
Needing an impartial audit of cycle time and quality
Wanting a human-in-the-loop AI workflow for research and drafts

faq.q: What is the first deliverable in a content operations engagement?
faq.a: The first deliverable is a mapped workflow showing all seven stages, owners, tools and SLAs, plus a 90-day rollout plan with weekly checkpoints.

faq.q: How do you handle urgent requests that bypass the workflow?
faq.a: Define an expedited lane with a separate SLA, a dedicated approver and a cap on concurrent urgent items so the standard queue keeps moving.

faq.q: Can content operations work with existing tools?
faq.a: Yes. The engagement audits current stack, fills gaps with minimal new licences and builds integrations using Zapier or Make where native connections are missing.

faq.q: What role does AI play in content operations?
faq.a: AI assists with research, first drafts and image variants under a human-in-the-loop rule: every output is a draft until a named person approves it.

faq.q: How is pricing structured for content operations services?
faq.a: West Peek Productions scopes content operations work per engagement and does not publish a fixed price; send the scope for a quote.
